title: Deion Sanders sued by designer over rights to use ‘Prime’ logo
content:
A graphic designer in Nebraska has accused Colorado Buffaloes football coach Deion Sanders of using hollow promises to convince him to sign away all rights to two logos he says he created for Sanders’ personal brand.

Alan Tipp made the allegations in a January 2025 lawsuit he filed with the U.S. District Court in Nebraska, nearly 14 years after Sanders’ team first approached him about working together. Court records show Sanders, whose team disputes all of the lawsuit’s claims, was deposed late last month.

In his complaint, Tipp said he designed two logos for Sanders in 2011, shortly before the Pro Football Hall of Famer opened his Prime Prep Academy. Tipp said their relationship formed when Sanders contacted him after seeing his work in an Under Armour collaboration.

The logos, one of which says “Prime” and the other “Truth,” have appeared in branding partnerships involving Sanders. Sanders typically tagged and credited Tipp on any posts involving the logos, but the lawsuit said Tipp was never compensated for creating the designs.

Once Sanders agreed to take over Colorado’s football program in December 2022, the dynamic changed, and use of the logos became more widespread, the lawsuit states.

“Following Sanders’ appointment at the University of Colorado, the Works were reproduced on a myriad of clothing, which included, but was not limited to, ties for TwentyDollarTies.com, clothing and footwear produced, sold, and distributed by Nike, Under Armour, Dick’s, Scheels, Fanatics, and the University of Colorado Boulder; their reproduction on razors for Gillette, sunglasses for Blenders, motor vehicles affiliated with Jeep and Lamborghini, athletic and gym equipment, basketball courts, jewelry, hats; and in association with the Defendants’ partnerships and affiliations with Aflac, Nike, Amazon, Boost Mobile, Motorola, Blenders, Wear by Erin Andrews, and the University of Colorado Boulder,” the complaint states.

Tipp alleges that around that time, Sam Morini, Sanders’ brand manager and talent agent for SMAC Entertainment, persuaded him to sign away all his rights to the designs. In exchange, Morini promised Tipp multiple work opportunities but did not follow through on any, the lawsuit alleges.

Morini allegedly told Tipp he would become a member of Sanders’ marketing team and gain access to Colorado players whom he could help build their own brands. Tipp said he was also told he could work directly with Nike on Sanders-related merchandise and apparel and would work on Sanders’ sunglasses line.

“Each of these statements were false at the time they were made and Morini, SMAC, and Sanders knew them to be false statements of fact, the purpose of which was to induce Tipp to sign the Agreement,” the lawsuit reads. “Shortly after Tipp executed the Agreement, Sanders and his representatives began evading Tipp.”

Tipp’s lawsuit argues the false promises constitute fraud and that Sanders’ team never intended to work with him once they secured his signature. He is asking for a jury to void the rights transfer and award him more than $75,000 in damages. His complaint points to revenue from the sunglasses, which the lawsuit says exceeded $5 million in their first three days on sale. Tipp admits not being sure how much total money Sanders made off the design.

Sanders argued in a court declaration attributed to him and filed Friday that he had used the logos before Tipp claims the two agreed to work together. Sanders does not refer to Tipp by name, instead pointing to the logos being rooted in an endorsement deal he signed with Under Armour in 2011 and saying “no one at Under Armour, or anyone else, objected to my use of these logos until this lawsuit was filed.”

If all his requests are granted, Tipp’s lawsuit would end efforts by Sanders’ Prime Time Enterprises to trademark various forms of “Prime” stylizations. They would be banned from using Tipp’s design going forward.

Attorneys for Sanders and SMAC Entertainment were not immediately available for comment. They have requested that the judge issue a summary judgment rather than take the case to trial.
